deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft for a lecture course on definite integrals with complex limits. The previous page is headed 'Riemann 18' and begins 'Wir wollen heute übergehen zu den Integralen zwischen imaginären Grenzen'. This page carries a lecture timetable note ('Donnerstags, Freitags und Sonnabends von 1-2 Uhr'). The next page is a letter draft dated 4 April 1859. The page sketches, in note form, the standard route from complex numbers to the residue/principal-value formula.

(1) Terminology. Gauss gave numbers a+b√-1 the name 'complex numbers'. Riemann then lists the parts: real part, imaginary part, and conjugate. In the margin he sets the Latin pairs numerus abstractus / numerus concretus against complexus / incomplexus, apparently glossing the origin of the word 'complex'.

(2) Definition of a function of a complex variable and the Cauchy-Riemann equations. Write w=u+iv, z=x+iy. Require dw/dz to be the same whether dz=dx or dz=i dy. This gives ∂w/∂x = ∂w/∂(iy), i.e.
 u_x + i v_x = u_y/i + v_y = v_y - i u_y.
Comparing real and imaginary parts gives u_x = v_y and v_x = -u_y; both are written on the page.

(3) Example w=1/z². With z=re^{iφ}, w = r^{-2}e^{-2iφ}, so u = cos2φ/r² and v = -sin2φ/r². The page writes '1/rr cos2φ (+ ...)' and '-1/rr sin2φ'. The X-shaped sketch with '+' in two opposite sectors is the sign pattern of u=cos2φ/r²: positive for |φ|<π/4 and in the opposite sector. A partly erased attempt to verify the CR equations for this example stands next to it.

(4) The integral. ∫_{(a)}^{(b)} f(z)dz = ∫(u+iv)(dx+i dy) = ∫(u dx - v dy) + i∫(v dx + u dy). The claim, partly legible, is that this depends only on the endpoints. The lens-shaped sketch shows two paths from a to b.

(5) Proof via Green's theorem. Set Φ = ∫_{(c,0)}^{(x,y)} X dx + Y dy, so dΦ = X dx + Y dy. Riemann evaluates ∬(∂Y/∂x - ∂X/∂y)dx dy strip by strip: a horizontal strip of width dy meets the boundary at points 1,2,3,4. Integrating ∂Y/∂x along the strip gives (-Y' + Y'' - Y''' + Y^{IV})dy. With the orientation convention ∂y = ∓dy at the crossings (my reading), this is the boundary integral ∮Y dy; a crossed-out line does the same for X dx with vertical strips.

Applying this to the two real line integrals (my completion):
- For X=u, Y=-v the integrand is -(v_x+u_y)=0.
- For X=v, Y=u it is u_x - v_y = 0 (the page writes ∬(∂u/∂x - ∂v/∂y)dxdy).
Hence the integral over a closed curve vanishes where f is regular. The figure with axes shows a region crossed by horizontal and vertical strips, with a small circle cut out around a singular point.

(6) Singularities. The second figure is a region containing several singular points, enclosed in small circles joined by cuts, inside a larger curve. The marginal '2π', 'cos2φ/rr' and '∂v/∂x' suggest a check that the circle integral of 1/z² is zero: ∫_0^{2π} cos2φ dφ = 0. This is my inference.

(7) Integral through a pole on the real path. Consider P = ∫_{a+0i}^{b+0i} f(z)/z dz with a<0<b; the sketch shows the segment a—b indented by a small semicircle over 0. Using ∫dz/z = log r + iφ and dz/z = i dφ on a circle:
- Over the upper semicircle traversed from φ=π to φ=0, ∫ f(z)/z dz → -πi·p, where p = lim z·(f(z)/z) = f(0).
- So the indented-path integral equals lim(∫_a^{-ε} + ∫_{ε}^b) f(z)/z dz - πi p, i.e. principal value minus πi p.
- Over a full closed curve around 0, ∮ f(z)/z dz = 2πi p, which is the final formula '∫ f(z) dz = 2πi p' in the residue sense. The last wavy closed curve illustrates this.

A small arrow sketch near '-πi' probably indicates the normal/orientation convention.
errors: In the 1/z² example the line '∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y = (1/z²) = 1/rr cos2φ + sin2φ' is garbled shorthand. Correctly, u = cos2φ/r² and v = -sin2φ/r², while ∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y = Re(-2/z³) = -2cos3φ/r³. The '+ sin2φ' lacks the factor 1/r² and the i/sign, though v = -sin2φ/rr is written correctly below.
The strip sum (-Y'+Y''-Y'''+Y^{IV})dy implicitly assumes a horizontal line meets the boundary in finitely many (here four) points; this is standard and acceptable in a lecture sketch.

The final formula is written '∫ f z dz = 2πi p'. Given the preceding lines, the integrand should be f(z)/z, or else p should be read as the residue of f. This is a notational abbreviation rather than a mathematical error.
The sign of the semicircle term (-πi p) presupposes the indentation passes above 0, traversed from -ε to +ε; this is consistent with the sketch.

results.what: Derivation of u_x=v_y, v_x=-u_y from direction-independence of dw/dz (∂w/∂x = ∂w/∂(iy))
results.usually_credited_to: d'Alembert (1752), Euler, Cauchy (1814/1825); Riemann's 1851 dissertation makes them the definition of a complex function

results.what: Path independence of ∫f(z)dz via the double-integral (Green) identity computed strip by strip
results.modern_name: Cauchy integral theorem via Green's theorem
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (1825); the Green-theorem proof is in Riemann's dissertation (1851)

results.what: Indented contour through a pole: path integral equals principal value minus πi f(0); full loop gives 2πi f(0)
results.modern_name: Sokhotski-Plemelj half-residue / indentation lemma; residue theorem / Cauchy integral formula
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (1825-1831); Sokhotski (1873) and Plemelj (1908) for the general boundary-value form

results.what: Etymological remark linking 'complex' to numerus abstractus/concretus, complexus/incomplexus

deep.surprise_reason: This is standard Cauchy-style complex integration as presented in Riemann's known lectures on definite integrals and complex functions. The CR equations, Green-theorem proof of path independence, and the half-residue for an indented path are all routine for him. Only minor pedagogical details (the etymological gloss, the lecture timetable, dating to around 1859) are of archival interest.

checkable.sympy: x,y=symbols('x y',real=True); w=1/(x+I*y)**2; u=simplify(re(expand_complex(w))); v=simplify(im(expand_complex(w))); [simplify(diff(u,x)-diff(v,y)), simplify(diff(v,x)+diff(u,y))]
checkable.asserts: 1/z^2 satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations (both entries are 0).
u = cos2φ/r^2 and v = -sin2φ/r^2 for w = 1/z^2 (result is 0).
The circle integral of cos2φ vanishes (=0), consistent with ∮dz/z^2 = 0.
The upper semicircle from -ε to +ε contributes ∫dz/z = -πi.
Example of the indented formula with f=e^z, p=f(0)=1: the indented integral from -1 to 2 equals PV - πi = Ei(2) - Ei(-1) - πi.

transcription_corrections: 'numerus abstractus / numerus concretus' may read 'numeri abstracti / numeri concreti' (Latin endings unclear); they are paired against 'Complexus / incompl.'.
'z f(z)(z) = p' should be read as 'z·f(z)/z = p', i.e. p = lim_{z→0} z·(f(z)/z) = f(0), the residue.
'=Y²dy' is more likely '=Y′dy' or a boundary-value notation; it is not a square.
The line under the f(z)dz integral is roughly 'hängt [bloß/nur] ab von seinen Grenzen' (the integral depends only on its limits); the machine reading is fragmentary.
In '∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y = (1/z²) = 1/rr cos2φ + sin2φ' the bracket likely denotes a derivative or real part; the line is a rough working note.
The X-shaped sketch with two '(+)' marks is the sign diagram of cos2φ, not text.
